\chapter{Good and So-So}
\label{ch:pa-good-and-soso}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer how are you with changa or thik-thak, say why changa's origin is disputed rather than settled, name echo reduplication as the habit that made thak, and write both Gurmukhi consonants of changa.}

The reader produces the middling answer, states that its second half carries no meaning outside the pair, names echo reduplication as the machine that made it, and runs all three wellbeing answers against each other.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[changā]{changā — good, and a trail that stops}

\label{lesson:PA-C32-changa}



\begin{quote}
Ask \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?} aloud, then answer it the way you first learned to: \emph{ṭhīk}. That answer reports a state — nothing is wrong. This chapter adds the answer that reports a judgement — things are good.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\emph{changā} — \textbf{good}
\end{quote}

The middle carries a hum through the nose, the sound the small mark \textbf{\pa{ੰ}} writes in \textbf{\pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ}}. Say it as \emph{chan-gā}, letting the nose take the \emph{n}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Every word taken apart so far has ended somewhere: \emph{bhrātṛ} for brother, \emph{kṛp-} for what is coming two chapters from now, *\emph{kerh\textsubscript{2}-} for the head. \emph{Changā} goes back one step to a Middle Indo-Aryan \textbf{caṅga}, \textquotedblleft{}fine, handsome,\textquotedblright{} and then the trail stops.

Scholars have proposed two continuations and settled on neither. One reads \emph{caṅga} as inherited Indo-Aryan; the other reads it as an early borrowing from a Dravidian language of the south. Both are argued in print. Neither is proved.

That is worth meeting head-on rather than papering over, because the two-source story this book keeps telling — Sanskrit on one side, Persian and Arabic on the other — has a third possibility underneath it. India's oldest language family was neither, and words moved between them long before anything was written down. \emph{Changā} may be one of those.

Two answers are now available for the same question. \emph{Ṭhīk} says nothing is wrong. \emph{Changā} says things are good. Add \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}} to either and the answer becomes respectful.

On the page, \emph{changā} needs two letters this book has not taught. They arrive in this chapter, one at a time.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{changā}, with the hum through the nose
  \item \emph{Answer:} \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?} with \emph{changā jī}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{ṭhīk} (nothing wrong) and \emph{changā} (good)
  \item \emph{State:} where the trail behind \emph{changā} stops, and the two proposals for what lies beyond
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for good. (\emph{Changā}.) Answer the wellbeing question with it, respectfully. (\emph{Changā jī}.) How far back can it be traced with confidence? (To \emph{caṅga}, and no further.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%9A\%E0\%A9\%B0\%E0\%A8\%97\%E0\%A8\%BE}{Wiktionary: changa}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%9A\%E0\%A4\%82\%E0\%A4\%97\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: changa (Hindi)}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cha]{\pa{ਚ} — the quiet twin of \pa{ਛ}}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-chacha}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\pa{ਛ}} once from memory and say \emph{chha}, with the puff of breath. Then say \emph{changā} aloud. The first sound of \emph{changā} is the same mouth-shape with the puff taken away.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one letter}
Trace \textbf{\pa{ਚ}} twice and say \emph{cha}. Set it beside \textbf{\pa{ਛ}} once and look at what separates them: Gurmukhi writes the breath as an extra stroke, so a heavier shape means a heavier puff of air.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover both models. Write \textbf{\pa{ਚ}}, then \textbf{\pa{ਛ}}. Compare only which one carries the extra stroke.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two letters, one difference. Nothing else changes.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭhīk-ṭhāk]{ṭhīk-ṭhāk — half a word, and it is the important half}

\label{lesson:PA-C32-thik-thak}



\begin{quote}
Two answers to \emph{how are you} are already yours: \emph{ṭhīk}, nothing wrong; \emph{changā}, good. Write \textbf{\pa{ਚ}} once while you say them, so the letter from the last session stays warm.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ṭhīk-ṭhāk} — \textbf{so-so, getting by}
\end{quote}

Both halves start with the tongue curled back against the roof of the mouth, then release with a puff. The vowel is the only thing that changes: \emph{ṭhīk}, \emph{ṭhāk}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Look for \emph{ṭhāk} in a dictionary and it will not be there on its own. It exists to answer \emph{ṭhīk}, and nowhere else.

This is \textbf{echo reduplication}, and it runs through the whole subcontinent. A speaker takes a word, repeats it with one sound changed, and the pair means something the single word did not: a loosened, approximate, and-things-of-that-sort version of itself. \emph{Ṭhīk} is a firm fine. \emph{Ṭhīk-ṭhāk} is a fine with a shrug in it — well enough, nothing to report.

English keeps a handful of these frozen — \emph{okey-dokey}, \emph{helter-skelter}, \emph{hocus-pocus} — but an English speaker cannot make a fresh one and expect to be understood. A Punjabi speaker can, on the spot, from almost any noun.

So this entry teaches two things at once: an answer you can give, and a machine for making more.

Three answers now sit side by side. \emph{Changā}: good. \emph{Ṭhīk}: nothing wrong. \emph{Ṭhīk-ṭhāk}: getting by.

On the page this word needs one letter still to come, which arrives in the next chapter. Until then it stays in the ear.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṭhīk-ṭhāk}, both halves curled back
  \item \emph{State:} what \emph{ṭhāk} means on its own (nothing — it exists to echo)
  \item \emph{Run through:} the three wellbeing answers — \emph{changā}, \emph{ṭhīk}, \emph{ṭhīk-ṭhāk}
  \item \emph{Name:} one English pair built the same way (\emph{okey-dokey}, \emph{helter-skelter})
  \item \emph{Recall:} what Sanskrit \emph{accha} described (clear water), and the particle behind \emph{nā} (*\emph{ne})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the middling answer. (\emph{Ṭhīk-ṭhāk}.) Which half is a real word? (The first.) Name the habit that made the second. (Echo reduplication.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%A0\%E0\%A9\%80\%E0\%A8\%95}{Wiktionary: thik}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/echo\_word}{Wiktionary: echo word}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ga]{\pa{ਗ} — third in the throat row}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-gagga}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਖ}} once each. Both are made at the back of the mouth: \emph{ka} dry, \emph{kha} with breath. Then write \textbf{\pa{ਚ}} once, from the session before this one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one letter}
Trace \textbf{\pa{ਗ}} twice and say \emph{ga}. It is made in the same place as \textbf{\pa{ਕ}}, with the voice switched on — put a finger on your throat and feel it hum on \emph{ga} and go quiet on \emph{ka}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the models. Write \textbf{\pa{ਕ}}, then \textbf{\pa{ਗ}}. Compare only the new shape.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You can now write both consonants of \emph{changā}. The word itself is assembled in the next chapter.
\end{tcolorbox}
